One night under the moonlight, he chanted at length,
claiming to have captured the style and manner of the worthies of old.
Xiè Zhān always praised him from afar.
Kǎi Zhī, receiving this,
exerted himself even more tirelessly.
When Zhān was about to sleep,
he told the person massaging his feet to take his place.
Kǎi Zhī did not notice the change
and continued almost until dawn before stopping."
Yīn Zhòngwén's talent was broad and far-reaching.
The *Xù Jìn Yángqiū* (Continuation of the Annals of the Jìn Dynasty) says:
"Zhòngwén was refined and talented,
writing dozens of articles."
And though he did not read widely,
Bó Liàng sighed and said: Liàng,
"A different view."
"If Yīn Zhòngwén had read half as much as Yuán Bào,
Qiū Zhī's "Preface to Essays" says:
"Bào's style name was Shìwèi,
a native of Chén Commandery.
His grandfather was Dān,
Grand Administrator of Lìyáng.
His father was Zhì,
Intendant of Lángyé.
During the Lóng'ān era, Bào was a junior scribe,
and successively promoted to Chief Clerk to the Grand Commandant,
and Administrator of Dānyáng.
He died in the ninth year of Yìxī."
His talent was no less than that of Bān Gù."
The "Later Book of Han" says:
"Gù's style name was Mèngjiān,
a native of Yòu Fúfēng.
From a young age, he possessed outstanding talent,
learning without a constant teacher,
and excelled at composition.
He thoroughly studied all the classics and commentaries."
Yáng Fú composed "Ode to Snow," saying:
"Endowed with purity to transform,
Riding the air to flutter.
Encountering form, it displays brilliance,
"And thus, cleanliness becomes brilliance."
Huán Yìn subsequently used it to write on fans.
*Zhongxing Shu* says:
"Yìn, zi Màozǔ,
was from Qiáo State.
His grandfather was Chōng,
Grand Commandant.
His father was Sì,
Governor of Jiangzhou.
Yìn had pure conduct from a young age,
and was known for his tranquility and withdrawal.
He served up to the position of Director of the Palace Library.
After Xuán's defeat,
he was exiled to Ancheng Commandery,
and later executed."
Wáng Xiàobó was strolling in the capital,
and arrived in front of his younger brother Wáng Dǔ's house.
Dǔ was the childhood name of Wáng Shuǎng.
*Zhongxing Shu* says:
"Shuǎng, zi Jìmíng,
was the fourth younger brother of Gōng.
He served up to the position of Attendant in Ordinary.
After Gōng's affair failed,
he was posthumously awarded Grand Master of Ceremonies."
He asked:
"Which line in ancient poetry is the best?"
Dǔ thought but had not yet answered.
Xiào Bó
praised, "‘Suǒ yù wú gù wù,
yān dé bù sù lǎo?’
This line is excellent."
Huán Xuán once ascended the South Tower of the city of Jiānglíng and said,
"I now wish to compose a eulogy for Wáng Xiàobó."
He then chanted and sighed for a long time,
and then began to write.
Within the space of a single gathering,
the eulogy was completed.
The "Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn" state:
"Huán Xuán's literary beauty
surpassed that of his generation."
The "Collected Works of Xuán" contains his "Eulogy Preface," which states:
"On the seventeenth day of the ninth month of the second year of Lóng'ān,
the former General of the Vanguard, and Inspector of the two provinces of Qīng and Yǎn, Wáng Xiàobó of Tàiyuán, passed away.
The mountains and rivers brought forth a divine spirit,
a wise man was nurtured.
But his spirit was extinguished,
and he did not bequeath his blessings.
The Way of Heaven is obscure,
who can fathom its ups and downs?
Even dogs and horses turn around to bite,
and jackals and wolves stand on dry land.
The peaks crumble the tall wutong trees,
and the forests destroy the old bamboo.
When a man dies,
the state loses its shepherd.
How shall we eulogize him?
Let us extol his fragrant virtues."
There was much more written,
not all of which is recorded.
When Huán Xuán first annexed Western Xia,
governing Jing,
and Jiang two provinces,
two prefectures and one kingdom.
The "Separate Biography of Xuan" says:
"After Xuan defeated Yīn Zhòngkān,
and later Yáng Quánqí,
he sent envoys to hint to the court,
and the court appointed Xuan as governor of eight provinces,
concurrently holding the positions of governor of Jiangzhou,
and Jingzhou."
At that time, it began to snow,
and congratulatory messages arrived from five locations,
with five sets of written submissions all coming in.
Huán Xuán was in the listening hall,
answering each submission as it arrived.
The responses were all brilliantly structured,
without any confusion or mixing.
When Huán Xuán went to the capital,
Yáng Fú was serving as the assistant administrator of Yanzhou,
Someone came from the capital to visit his door.
The letter said:
"Since long ago, due to worldly affairs, we have been separated,
and my innermost thoughts have been buried and suppressed.
Your Excellency reveals the morning light amidst accumulated darkness,
and clarifies hundreds of streams into a single source."
When Huán saw the letter,
he urgently summoned him forward,
saying:
"Zǐdào,
Zǐdào,
why have you come so late?"
And immediately appointed him as Recorder and Military Advisor.
Mèng Chǎng was seen separately.
He became the Chief Clerk for Liú Láo zhī.
The *Continuation of the Spring and Autumn Annals of Jin* says:
"Láo zhī's courtesy name was Dàojiān,
a native of Péngchéng.
His family was prominent as generals for generations.
His father was Dùn,
General Who Conquers Barbarians.
Láo zhī was deep and resolute, with many plans,
and served as Military Advisor to Xiè Xuán.
In the campaign against Fú Jiān,
he achieved success through his bravery and fierceness.
And when he pacified Wáng Gōng,
he was promoted to Governor of Xú Province.
When Huán Xuán came down to the capital,
Yǐ Láo was made the vanguard,
and acted as General Who Conquers the West.
Xuán arrived to surrender,
and was employed as the Internal Administrator of Kuàijī.
He wanted to disband his troops,
(but Xuán) fled and hanged himself."
He went to the door to apologize,
and saw (the family) say,
"Lord Yáng,
Lord Yáng,
a hundred mouths rely on you!"
"How inhuman!
Having agreed with someone to travel together,
he abandoned him and left."
Yuán Fāng said,
"You agreed with my father to meet at midday.
If you don't arrive at midday,
that's being untrustworthy;
to scold your father in front of his son,
that's being impolite."
The friend was ashamed,
got out of the carriage and tried to pull him along.
Yuán Fāng entered the gate without looking back.
Zōng Shìlín of Nányáng,
was a contemporary of Wèi Wǔ,
but greatly disdained his character
and did not associate with him.
When Wèi Wǔ became Minister of Works
and oversaw the government,
he leisurely asked Zōng,
"Can we associate now?"
He replied,
"The will of the pine and cypress still remains."
Shìlín, having offended the emperor's will, was estranged,
and his position did not match his virtue.
The brothers of Emperor Wén often visited his door,
and all bowed alone under the bed,
such was the respect shown to him.
*Chǔ Guó Xiān Xián Zhuàn* (Biographies of Worthies of the State of Chu) says:
"Zōng Chéng, courtesy name Shìlín,
was a native of Ānzhòng in Nányáng.
His father, Zī,
had a fine reputation.
Chéng was young but cultivated virtue and was refined and upright,
truly standing out from the crowd.
He declined summons and appointments,
and those who came because of his virtue were as numerous as a forest.
When Wèi Wǔ (Cáo Cāo) was barely twenty,
he repeatedly visited his door.
However, the guests were always piled up,
and he was unable to get a word in.
So, he waited for Chéng to get up,
went to intercept him,
and, grabbing his hand, asked to befriend him.
Chéng refused and did not accept.
Later, the Emperor became Sīkōng (Minister of Works),
assisting the Hàn court.
He then said to Chéng:
'You used to disregard me,
can we now become friends?'
Chéng said:
'My will is still that of the pine and cypress.'
The Emperor was displeased,
but because of his reputation as a worthy,
he still treated him with respect.
He ordered Emperor Wén (Cáo Pī) to observe the rites of a junior towards him.
He appointed him, while still at home, as the Grand Administrator of Hànzhōng.
When Emperor Wǔ (Cáo Cāo) pacified Jì Province,
Chéng followed him to Yè.
Chén Qún and others all bowed to him.
The Emperor still harbored resentment over the old affair,
diminishing his position but honoring his treatment."
He would visit him at his home to inquire about matters of state,
seating him in the position of honor among his guests.
Emperor Wén summoned him to be a Grand Master of Upright Counsel.
Emperor Míng wished to promote him to the position of Chancellor,
but he firmly declined due to his age."
When Emperor Wèi Wén received the abdication,
Chén Qún bore a sorrowful expression.
The Emperor asked,
"I have received the Mandate of Heaven,
why are you not happy?"
Chén Qún replied,
"Your servant, along with Huá Xīn,
served the previous dynasty with deep respect.
Now, although I am pleased with Your Majesty's enlightened rule,
my sense of righteousness is still reflected in my countenance."
Huá Qiáo's "Genealogy Preface" says:
"When Wèi received the abdication,
the court officials, from the Three Dukes downwards,
were all granted titles and ranks.
Huá Xīn, because his demeanor displeased the times,
was moved to the position of Minister of Works,
without any advancement in rank.
Emperor Wén was unhappy for a long time
and asked the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Chén Qún,
'I have received the Mandate of Heaven,
and all the officials are delighted,
showing it in their voices and expressions;
yet the Chancellor and you alone seem not to be pleased.
Why is that?"
Qún rose from his seat, knelt at length, and said:
"Your servant and the Chancellor once served the Hàn dynasty.
Although our hearts are joyful,
propriety affects our countenance.
We also fear Your Majesty,
and truly expect to be resented."
The emperor was greatly pleased,
sighed for a long time,
and consequently esteemed them even more."
Guō Huái, as the Governor of Guānzhōng,
greatly won the hearts of the people
and also repeatedly had military achievements.
The *Wèi Zhì* says:
"Huái's courtesy name was Bójì,
he was a native of Yángqū in Tàiyuán.
During the Jiàn'ān period,
he was appointed as the Assistant of the Píngyuán Prefecture.
In the first year of Huángchū,
he was sent as an envoy to congratulate Emperor Wéndì on his ascension to the throne,
and remained delayed and could not catch up.
As the assembled ministers were celebrating,
the Emperor, with a stern expression, rebuked him, saying:
“In the past, when Yǔ met with the feudal lords at Túshān,
the Fángfēng clan arrived late,
and he immediately carried out a great execution.
Now, the whole world celebrates together,
yet you are the most delayed;
why is that?”
Huái said:
“I have heard that the Five Emperors prioritized teaching,
guiding the people with virtue.
When the Xià Dynasty's government declined,
they began to use penal laws.
Now I live in the era of Táng and
Yú,
and therefore knew I would be spared the execution of the Fángfēng clan.”
The Emperor was pleased by this response,
and promoted him to Inspector of Yōng Province,
and later to General Who Conquers the West.
Huái remained in Guānzhōng for more than thirty years,
and his achievements were remarkable.
He was promoted to Equal to the Three Excellencies and
posthumously granted the title of Grand General."
Huái's wife
was the younger sister of Grand Commandant Wáng Líng,
and was supposed to be executed along with Líng due to his affair.
The *Wèi Lüè* says:
Líng Zì Yàn Yún,
was from Qí in Tàiyuán.
He successively held the positions of Minister of Works,
Grand Commandant,
and General Who Conquers the East.
He secretly plotted to establish Chǔ Wáng Biāo,
but Sīmǎ Xuānwáng personally campaigned to suppress him.
Líng, binding himself, confessed his guilt.
He remotely said to the Grand Tutor:
"If you had simply summoned me with a brief note,
would I have failed to come?"
The Grand Tutor said:
"It is because you are not one who would submit to a brief note."
Thereupon he sent men to escort him west.
Líng, knowing his crime was grave,
tentatively asked for coffin nails
to observe the Grand Tutor's intentions.
The Grand Tutor provided them.
Líng, traveling to Xiàngchéng,
at night summoned his subordinates and said resolutely:
"I am eighty years old,
and my reputation and life will both be extinguished.
Is it fate!"
Thereupon he committed suicide.
The emissary's arrest and capture were extremely urgent,
Huái ordered preparations to be made,
fixing the date for departure.
The civil and military officials and common people of the prefecture urged Huái to raise troops,
Huái did not permit it.
When the date arrived,
he sent his wife away.
The common people wept and wailed, chasing after her, numbering tens of thousands.
After traveling several tens of *lǐ*,
Huái then ordered his attendants to pursue Madam and bring her back.
Thereupon, civil and military officials raced about,
as if it were a matter of life and death.
Once she arrived,
Huái wrote a letter to Xuān Dì, saying:
"My five sons are sorrowful and attached,
missing their mother.
If their mother is gone,
then there will be no five sons.
If the five sons perish,
then there will also be no Huái."
Xuān Dì then submitted a memorial,
specially pardoning Huái's wife.
The *Shì Yǔ* states:
"Huái's wife was to be punished as an accomplice,
and the supervising imperial censor went to arrest her.
The commanding generals and the chieftains of the Qiāng and Hú tribes kowtowed by the thousands,
requesting that Huái submit a memorial to retain his wife.
Huái did not comply.
As his wife departed,
none did not weep,
everyone wrung their wrists,
wanting to forcibly keep her.
Huái's five sons kowtowed and bled, begging for Huái.
Huái couldn't bear to watch,
so he ordered them to be chased back.
Thereupon, several thousand riders went to chase them back.
Huái wrote a letter to Sīmǎ Xuānwáng, saying:
"The five sons grieve for their mother,
and do not cherish their own lives.
If there were no mother,
there would be no five sons;
if the five sons were lost,
there would be no Huái either.
Now I have hastily chased them back.
If it is not in accordance with the law,
I will accept punishment from the authorities."
When the letter arrived,
Xuānwáng then memorialized to pardon him."
When Zhūgě Liàng arrived at the banks of the Wèi River,
Guānzhōng was shaken.
The *Shǔ Zhì* says:
"Liàng's courtesy name was Kǒngmíng,
he was from Yángdū, Lángyé.
He lived as a guest in Jīngzhōu,
personally plowing the fields,
and liked to compose the *Liáng Fǔ Yín*.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
and always compared himself to Guǎn Zhòng and
Yuè Yì,
At the time, people did not believe him.
Only Cuī Zhōupíng of Bólíng and
Xú Yuánzhí of Yǐngchuān said it was indeed so.
Xiānzhǔ was stationed at Xīnyě.
Xú Shù saw Xiānzhǔ and said:
"Zhūgě Kǒngmíng,
is a Sleeping Dragon.
Does the General wish to see him?"
Xiānzhǔ said:
"Come with him."
Shù said:
"This man can be visited,
but cannot be compelled to come."
Thereupon Xiānzhǔ went to see Liàng,
and said to Guān Yǔ and
Zhāng Fēi:
"For me to have Kǒngmíng
is like a fish having water."
He was repeatedly promoted to Prime Minister and
Governor of Yìzhōu.
He led troops on a northern expedition
and died in Wèinán."
Emperor Míng of Wèi greatly feared that Jìn Xuānwáng would engage in battle,
and thus sent Xīn Pí as Army Adjutant.
The *Wèi Zhì* says:
"Pí, styled Zuǒzhì,
was a native of Yángdǐ in Yǐngchuān.
He was repeatedly promoted to Commandant of the Guards."
Xuān Wáng 宣王, having already faced off with Liàng 亮 across the Wèi 渭 River and arrayed his troops,
Liàng 亮 employed deceptive schemes of all kinds.
Xuān Wáng 宣王 was indeed greatly angered,
and was about to respond with overwhelming force.
Liàng 亮 sent spies to observe him,
who returned and said,
"There is an old man,
resolutely holding a yellow battle-axe,
standing at the gate of the camp,
and the army is unable to come out."
Liàng 亮 said,
"This must be Xīn Zuǒzhì 辛佐治."
The *Jìn Yángqiū* 《晉陽秋》 states:
"Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮 invaded Méi 郿,
occupying the southern plains of the Wèi 渭 River.
An imperial edict ordered Gāozǔ 高祖 to resist him.
Liàng 亮 was skilled in soothing and controlling his troops,
and his military administration was strict and clear.
Moreover, the garrison troops were on a distant expedition,
and transporting grain was difficult and arduous.
Their advantage lay in field battles.
The court always, upon hearing of his (Liàng's 亮) movements,
wished to subdue him without fighting.
Gāozǔ 高祖 also thought this to be right.
However, possessing a large army to defend against external threats,
it was inappropriate to outwardly display a weak and fearful demeanor and diminish the overall morale.
Therefore, he fed the horses and donned armor,
always presenting an image of overwhelming force.
Although Liàng (Liàng) issued challenges,
he sometimes sent Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) women's headscarves and kerchiefs.
Headscarves and kerchiefs
are women's adornments.
He intended to provoke anger,
hoping to gain the advantage of Cáo Jiù (Cáo Jiù).
The court, worried that Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) would be unable to contain his indignation,
and because the Commandant of the Guards, Xīn Pí (Xīn Pí), was an upright minister,
the emperor sent Pí (Pí) to be Gāozǔ's (Gāozǔ) army adjutant, bearing the imperial staff.
Liàng (Liàng) indeed challenged again,
and Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) became enraged
and was about to go out to meet the challenge.
Pí (Pí) stood in the middle of the gate with the imperial staff,
and Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) stopped.
The officers and soldiers who heard and saw this were emboldened and became even more valiant.
Those who understand consider that even though a subject may command millions of troops, submitting to the royal envoy
displays a profound and far-reaching strategy,
and this is one such instance."
After Xiàhóu Xuán (Xiàhóu Xuán) was shackled,
the *Wèi Shì Chūnqiū* (魏氏春秋) says:
"Xuán's (Xuán) courtesy name was Tàichū (Tàichū),
he was a native of Qiáo (譙) state,
the son of Xiàhóu Shàng (Xiàhóu Shàng),
and the older brother of the Grand General's former wife.
His manner was lofty and bright,
his eloquence vast and unhindered.
During the Zhèngshǐ (正始) era,
he was a Protector of the Army.
After Cáo Shuǎng (Cáo Shuǎng) was executed,
he was summoned to be Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Knowing internally that he could not avoid punishment,
he did not engage in social activities,
nor did he keep writing implements.
When the Grand Tutor died,
Xǔ Yǔn said to Xuán,
"You have no more worries!"
Xuán sighed and said,
"Shìzōng,
why can't you see things?
This man especially treated me like a younger member of his extended family,
Zǐyuán and
Zǐshàng will not tolerate me."
Later, the Zhongshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat) Lǐ Fēng resented the Great General's control of the government,
and thus plotted to replace him with Xuán.
The Great General heard of this plot,
executed Fēng,
and arrested Xuán, sending him to the Tíngwèi (Court of Justice)."
Gān Bǎo's "Annals of Jin" says:
"Initially,
when Fēng was plotting,
he sent someone to inform Xuán.
Xuán replied,
'It is best to consider it carefully,
I will not report it.'
Therefore, he was involved in the disaster."
At that time, Zhōng Yù was the Tíngwèi (Court of Justice).
Zhōng Huì previously did not know Xuán,
but then became close to him.
Xuán said,
"Even though I am a person who has suffered punishment,
I dare not receive your orders!"
The "Shìyǔ" says:
"When Xuán arrived at the Ministry of Justice,
he was unwilling to submit a plea.
The Minister of Justice, Zhōng Yù, personally came to examine Xuán.
Xuán sternly said:
'What plea should I make?
Should I act as a clerk accusing someone?
You should write it for me.'
Yù considered Xuán to be a famous scholar,
whose integrity was too high to be bent,
but the trial had to be concluded.
At night, he wrote a plea for him,
ensuring it aligned with the facts.
He showed it to Xuán with tears in his eyes.
Xuán looked at it and said:
'Shouldn't it be like this?'"
Zhōng Huì was younger than Xuán.
Xuán did not associate with him.
That day, he became familiar with Xuán while sitting with Yù.
Xuán sternly said:
'Lord Zhōng,
how can you act like this!'"
The "Míngshì Zhuàn" says:
"Initially,
Xuán did not associate with Zhōng Yù because their aspirations were different.
Yù was the Minister of Justice.
Yù, as the Minister of Justice,
held Xián's hand and said:
'Tàichū, how could things have come to this?'
Xián sternly replied:
'Even if I were a person who has suffered castration,
I would not associate with you.'"
Note: Guō Bān was a person of the Western Jin Dynasty,
close to that era.
He wrote *A Worldly Account of Jin and Wei*,
and its contents are often detailed and accurate.
Sūn Shèng and his followers all adopted it when writing their books,
all saying that Xián distanced himself from Zhōng Huì.
However, Yuán Hóng's *Biographies of Famous Scholars* came out last,
not following previous history,
and instead claiming it was Zhōng Yù,
which can be called a mistake.
The records of his interrogation do not contain a single word [about such a thing],
and at the time of execution in the Eastern Market,
his countenance was no different.
The *Records of Wei* says:
"Xián's character was broad and generous,
and at the moment of execution,
his countenance was no different,
His demeanor was natural and unconstrained.
Xiàhóu Tàichū was on good terms with Chén Běn of Guǎnglíng.
Běn and Xuán were feasting and drinking in front of Běn's mother.
The *Shìyǔ* says:
"Běn's courtesy name was Xiūyuán,
he was from Dōngyáng in Línhuái."
The *Wèizhì* says:
"Běn was
from Dōngyáng in Guǎnglíng.
His father, Jiǎo,
was the Minister of Ceremonies (司徒 Sītú).
Běn served as a commandery governor,
and as Minister of Justice (廷尉 Tíngwèi).
In every position he held, he grasped the essential principles,
and focused on the big picture.
He was able to make his subordinates exert themselves to the fullest,
and he possessed the talent to lead and manage.
He did not concern himself with trivial matters,
nor did he study the laws,
yet he earned the title of Minister of Justice.
He was later promoted to General Who Pacifies the North (鎮北將軍 Zhènběi Jiāngjūn)."
Běn's younger brother, Qiān: the *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Qiān's courtesy name was Xiūyuān,
the second son of the Minister of Ceremonies.
He lacked a blunt and outspoken character,
but was witty and full of resourcefulness.
He rose in office to Grand Marshal (大司馬 Dà Sīmǎ)."
Returning,
he went straight in,
reaching the hall door.
Tàichū then rose and said,
"It can be shared,
but it cannot be mixed."
The *Biographies of Famous Men* says:
"Xuán valued seniority within his village;
he did not originally consider virtue or position;
he would definitely bow to those who were older.
Once, he was drinking in front of Chén Běn's mother,
when Qiān came, he went out.
This is an example of something that can be shared
but cannot be mixed."
The Duke of Gāoguìxiāng died,
and there was an uproar both inside and outside the court.
The *Records of Wei* says:
"The Duke of Gāoguìxiāng's personal name was Máo,
his courtesy name was Yànshì,
the grandson of Emperor Wén,
and the son of Lín, the Prince Dìng of Dōnghǎi.
He was initially enfeoffed as the Count of Tán.
The Duke of Gāoguìxiāng loved learning and matured early.
When the Prince of Qí was deposed,
the officials welcomed him,
and he ascended the throne as emperor."
The *Spring and Autumn Annals of Han and Jin* says:
"After the affair of Cáo Fāng,
the people of Wèi simplified and reduced the palace guards,
with no more armor and weapons.
The military personnel at the various gates
were old and weak.
Cáo Máo, seeing his authority diminish day by day,
could not contain his anger.
He summoned the court attendant Wáng Shěn,
the minister Wáng Jīng,
and the attendant gentleman Wáng Yè and said:
'Sīmǎ Zhāo's intentions
are known to everyone.
I cannot sit idly and accept being deposed.
Today, I will personally lead you to punish him.'
Wáng Jīng advised against it, but he would not listen.
He then took out a wooden tablet from his robe and threw it on the ground, saying:
'My decision is made!
Even if I die,
what regret is there?
Moreover, there is no certainty of death!'
Thereupon, he went to inform the Empress Dowager.
Shěn and Yè ran to inform Zhāo,
and Zhāo prepared for it.
Máo then led several hundred pages and servants,
clamoring and went out.
Zhāo's younger brother, the Commandant of Tunqi Cavalry Zhòu, entered
and encountered Máo at the East Zhǐchē Gate.
The guards shouted at him,
The armored troops scattered and fled.
The Central Protector of the Army, Jiǎ Chōng, then confronted Máo,
fighting below the Southern Gate.
Máo personally wielded his sword,
and the soldiers wanted to retreat.
The Crown Prince's attendant, Chéng Jì, asked Chōng,
"The situation is critical!
What should we do?"
Chōng said,
"The Duke has supported you all,
precisely for today.
In today's matter,
there is nothing to ask."
Jì immediately went forward and stabbed Máo,
the blade exiting his back."
The "Spring and Autumn Annals of Wei" says:
"The Emperor intended to execute the Grand General,
and ordered the officials to again advance him to the position of Chancellor,
adding the nine bestowments.
The Emperor himself at night led the superfluous attendant Lǐ Zhāo,
and the Yellow Gate attendant Jiāo Bó, and others down from the Língyún Terrace,
armor and weapons were given out,
intending to seize the opportunity,
sending envoys to personally issue a punitive expedition,
but it rained and they retreated.
The next day,
he then met with Wáng Jīng and others,
and took out a yellow silk edict from his bosom, saying:
"This is tolerable?
What is not tolerable?"
"Now is the time to resolutely carry out this matter."
The emperor then drew his sword and ascended the imperial carriage,
leading the palace guards, sleeping quarters officials, and low-ranking servants,
beating the war drum,
and exiting Yúnlóng Gate.
Jiǎ Chōng entered from the outside,
and the imperial troops scattered.
The emperor still proclaimed himself the Son of Heaven,
wielding his sword and fiercely attacking,
and none dared to approach.
Jiǎ Chōng urged on the generals and soldiers,
and the cavalry commander Chéng Cuì and
his younger brother Jì advanced with spears.
The emperor died in battle.
At that time, there was a heavy rain,
with thunder and lightning obscuring the sky."
Sīmǎ Wénwáng asked the Palace Attendant Chén Tài,
"The *Wèi Zhì* says:
'Tài's courtesy name is Xuánbó,
son of the Minister of Works Qún.'"
"How can we pacify this?"
Tài said,
"Only by killing Jiǎ Chōng
to appease the world."
Wénwáng said,
"Can this matter be repeated?"
He replied:
"I only see what is above,
I do not see what is below."
Gān Bǎo's《Jìn Jì》 says:
"Concerning the assassination of Gāoguì Xiānggōng,
Sīmǎ Wénwáng summoned court officials to discuss the reason for it.
Grand Master of Ceremonies Chén Tài did not arrive.
He had his maternal uncle Xún Yǐ summon him,
asking if he could not come.
Tài said:
'The world discusses and
compares Tài to my maternal uncle,
but now my maternal uncle is not as good as Tài.'
His children and relatives, both inside and outside the family, all pressed him,
and he entered weeping.
Wénwáng received him in a private room,
and said:
'Xuánbó,
how should you advise me to deal with this?'
He replied:
'You can execute Jiǎ Chōng to apologize to the world.'
Wénwáng said:
'Think again for me and give me the next best option.'
Tài said:
'There is only advancement upon this;
I know of no other alternative.'
Wénwáng then stopped."
The《Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū》 says:
"When Cáo Máo died,
Sīmǎ Zhāo heard of it,
and threw himself on the ground, saying:
'What will the world say of me?'
Thereupon, he summoned the officials to discuss the matter.
Zhāo, with tears streaming down his face, asked Chén Tài:
'How should I place myself?'
Tài said:
'Your Excellency has brilliantly assisted several generations,
and your merit covers the world.
It was thought that you would emulate the ancients,
leaving behind a legacy of beauty for posterity.
To suddenly have the deed of killing a ruler,

Quickly execute Jiǎ Chōng,

Zhāo said:
'Gōng Lǘ cannot be executed;

Tài said sternly:
'My intention is only to advance this point;

The *Wèi Shì Chūn Qiū* says:

Hé Qiáo was respected by Emperor Wǔ,

Upon returning, he asked,

He replied,
"The Crown Prince's nature is as pure as ever."
The "Eulogies of Various Dukes of the Jin" says:

Gān Bǎo's "Annals of the Jin" says:

He was not the master of the entire world.

According to my research: Xún Yǐ was refined and elegant,
and by nature did not flatter.
Comparing these two accounts,
then Sūn Shèng's version is the correct one.
Zhūgě Jìng later entered the Jìn Dynasty,

Jìng said:

The *Zan* of the Dukes of Jin says:

*Hànshū* says:

Zàn's commentary says:

Others can make close relatives estranged,

Dù Yù went to Jīngzhōu,

Wáng Yǐn's *Book of Jìn* says:
"Yù's courtesy name was Yuánkǎi,

Yù (魏預)'s wisdom and resourcefulness were profound,

Chángyú embraced the inner chariot,

When Dù Yù was appointed General Who Pacifies the South,

At that time, there was also Péi Shūzé.
Yáng Zhìshū arrived late and

During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,

Hé Qiáo served as the Director of the Secretariat.
According to custom,

Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" said:

Later, the official carriage arrived,

The practice of providing separate carriages for the Director and the Magistrate began from this point.

Shān Gōng's eldest son wore a short cap

Xiàng Xióng was the Hé Nèi Zhǔbù (Clerk of Hé Nèi).
Because some official business did not involve Xióng,
the governor Liú Huái was angered and
Consequently, he dismissed him with a staff.

This, then, is not Liú Huái.

'If you do good,
good people will resent it.'
She replied:
'In that case, should I do bad?'
He said:
'Good is already not to be done,
how much the more so bad?'"
Empress Jǐngxiàn, of the Yáng clan, said:
"Although these words are coarse,
they can instruct the people of the world."
Xǔ Yǔn's wife was the daughter of the Commandant Ruan,
named Derú.
The *Wèi L略* says:
"Xǔ Yǔn, style Shìzōng,
was a person from Gāoyáng.
In his youth, along with Cuī Zàn of Qīnghé,
he gained fame in Jì Province.
He served, reaching the position of General of the Central Army."
The *Chén Liú Zhìmíng* says:
"Ruǎn Gòng, style Bóyàn,
was a person from Wèishì.
He was pure and sincere, upholding the Dao,
and acted with propriety and yielding.
He served in the Wèi,
He reached the position of Wèi Wèi Qīng (衛尉卿, Commandant of the Guards).
His youngest son, Kǎn (侃),
styled Dé Rú (德如),
possessed outstanding talent,
and was adorned with a reputation for reason and principle.
His demeanor was elegant and refined,
and he was friends with Jī Kāng (嵇康).
He served as Tài Shǒu (太守, Governor) of Hénèi (河內).
(Ruan) Yǔn (阮允) was remarkably ugly.
After the marriage ceremony concluded,
Yǔn (允) showed no intention of returning inside,
causing his family deep concern.
It happened that Yǔn (允) had a guest arrive,
and his wife ordered a maid to observe him.
The maid returned and reported,
"It is Master Huán (桓郎)."
This Master Huán (桓郎) was
Huán Fàn (桓範).
The *Wèi Lüè* (魏略, Brief History of Wei) states:
"Fàn (範), styled Yǔn Míng (允明),
was a native of Pèi Jùn (沛郡).
He served as Dà Sī Nóng (大司農, Grand Minister of Agriculture)
and was executed by (Sīmǎ) Xuān Wáng (宣王)."
The wife said,
"Do not worry,
Huán (桓) will surely persuade him to come in."
Huán (桓) indeed said to Xǔ Yǔn (許允),
"The Ruǎn (阮) family has married such an ugly daughter to you,
Therefore, there must be a reason;
you should observe it."
Xǔ then turned and went inside.
After he saw his wife,
he immediately wanted to leave.
His wife, realizing that if he left this time,
there would be no chance of him returning,
then grabbed his garment to stop him."
Xǔ then said to her:
"A wife has four virtues;
how many do you possess?"
The *Zhou Li* states:
"The nine *pín* are in charge of the methods of female education,
to teach the nine *yù*.
Female virtue,
female speech,
female appearance,
female work."
Zhèng's commentary states:
"Virtue means chastity and obedience,
speech means appropriate language,
appearance means gentleness,
work means silk and hemp."
The wife said:
"The only thing this new wife lacks is appearance.
However, a scholar has a hundred virtues;
how many do you possess?"
Xǔ said:
"All of them."
The wife said:
"Of the hundred virtues of a man, virtue is the most important.
You love beauty but not virtue;
how can you say you possess all of them?"
Yǔn had a look of shame,
and they subsequently respected each other.
Xǔ Yǔn 許允 was appointed as the Lìbù Láng 吏部郎 (Director of the Ministry of Personnel).
He mostly employed people from his hometown.
Emperor Wèi Míngdì 魏明帝 sent the Hubēn 虎賁 (Imperial Guards) to arrest him.
His wife came out and warned Xǔ Yǔn 許允, saying:
"[Míngzhǔ kěyǐ lǐ duó,] ("An enlightened ruler can be persuaded with reason.")
[Nán yǐ qíng qiú.]" ("But is difficult to sway with emotion.")
After he arrived,
the emperor interrogated him closely.
Xǔ Yǔn 許允 replied:
"[Jǔ ěr suǒ zhī.]" ("'Promote those you know.'")
"[Chén zhī xiāngrén,] ("These are the people from my hometown.")
[Chén suǒ zhī yě.]" ("Those I know.")
"[Bìxià jiǎnxiào wèi chènzhí yǔ bù?] ("Does Your Majesty find they are competent or not?")
[Ruò bù chènzhí,] ("If they are not competent.")
[Chén shòu qí zuì.]" ("I will accept the punishment.")
After inspection,
it was found that all the officials were well-suited to their positions,
so he was released.
Xǔ Yǔn's 許允 clothing was tattered,
An imperial edict bestowed new clothing.
Initially, when Yǔn was arrested,
his entire family wailed.
Ruǎn, the new wife, calmly said,
"Do not worry,
he will return soon."
She prepared millet congee to wait.
After a short time, Yǔn arrived.
The *Wèi Shì Chūnqiū* states:

when Yǔn was serving as an official in the Ministry of Personnel,

Emperor Míngdì suspected that his selections were not in proper order

Yǔn's wife, of the Ruǎn family, went out barefoot,

'A wise ruler can be swayed by reason,
but not by emotional appeals.'
Yǔn nodded in agreement and went in.
The emperor angrily questioned him,
and Yǔn replied,
'Although the term of the commandery administrator of a certain commandery was at its limit,
the documents arrived first,
so his term limit came later,
but the date limit came earlier.'
The emperor then took the matter to examine it,
and was thus appeased.
After sending him out,
he looked at his tattered clothing,
and said,
'He is a clean official.'"
Xǔ Yǔn was executed by Jìn Jǐngwáng.
A student ran in to inform his wife.
His wife was at her loom,
her expression did not change,
she said:
"I knew it long ago!"
The *Wèi Zhì* says:
"Initially,
the commander (lǐngjūn) was close to Xiàhóu Xuán and
Lǐ Fēng.
Someone fraudulently made an edict that was one chi and one cun long,

Before long,
someone rode a horse before dawn and gave Yǔn the imperial decree,
the gatekeeper said:
'There is an imperial decree.'

Yǔn threw the letter in the fire and burned it,

The *Wèi Lüè* says:
"The following year,
Lǐ Fēng was arrested,
Yǔn wanted to go to see the General-in-Chief.
Having already left the gate,

The General-in-Chief heard of this and found it strange, saying:
'I myself am arresting Lǐ Fēng,
Why are the scholar-officials in such a flurry?"
Subsequently, the General Who Guards the North, Liú Jìng, passed away,

The Grand General wrote to Yǔn, saying:
"Although the position of General Who Guards the North involves few matters,

Considering your experience in shaking the resounding drum,
raising the vermilion staff,
and serving throughout your home province,
this is what is meant by displaying embroidered chopsticks during the day."
Subsequently, the authorities reported that Yǔn had previously, without authorization, used provisions and grain from the kitchen
to request favors for various performers and their officials.
He was to have his death sentence reduced to banishment to the frontier,
but he died on the way."
The *Wèi Shì Chūnqiū* says:
"When Yǔn became General Who Guards the North,
he happily said to his wife:
'I know I am spared!'
His wife said:
'Disaster is evident in this;
how can you say you are spared?'"
The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* says:
"Yǔn had upright feelings,
and disagreed with Emperor Wéndì,
so he was imprisoned and killed."
The *Fùrén Jí* (Collection of Women) records a letter from the Ruan woman to Yǔn,
describing the cause of Yǔn's misfortune.
The wording is very sad and heart-wrenching.
Much of the text is not recorded here.
His disciples wanted to hide his children.
The woman said:
"Do not involve the children in this matter."
Later, they moved to live near his tomb.
Prince Jǐng sent Zhōng Huì to observe them,
to see if their talent surpassed their father's,
in which case they would be arrested.
The children consulted their mother.
The mother said:
"Although you are good,
your talents are not great.
If you speak frankly and from the heart,
there will be nothing to worry about.
Do not grieve excessively;
stop when Huì stops.
Also, ask as little as possible about court affairs."
The children followed her advice.
Huì instead reported their situation truthfully,
and in the end, they were spared.
The *Shì Yǔ* (Tales of the World) says:

The court, because Qí came from a family that had suffered misfortune,

Emperor Shìzǔ issued an edict,

Wáng Gōngyuān married the daughter of Zhūgě Dàn.

The wife replied:

The *Wèi Zhì* states:

Your servant believes that Wáng Guǎng was a renowned scholar;

This statement is incorrect.
Wáng Jīng was poor in his youth.
He rose in office to two thousand piculs of grain.
His mother said to him,

Jīng did not heed her words.
He became a palace secretary

He was disloyal to Jìn

Weeping, he took his leave of his mother, saying,

His mother showed no sorrowful expression at all

The *Shì Yǔ* says:

During the trouble with the Gāoguì Xiānggōng,
Wáng Shěn and

Jīng, because of his uprightness, did not go out.
Because Shěn and
Yè stated his intentions,

The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* says:
"Shěn and
Yè were about to leave,

disregarding the principles of right and wrong.
This has not been a matter of a single day.

Máo did not listen.
Later, he killed Jīng,

As he was about to die,

His mother's expression did not change,

To die together with this,

Gān Bǎo's *Jìn Jì* says:
"Jīng was upright
but not loyal to me,
gù zhū zhī." "Therefore, he was executed."
According to what Fù Chì

then Jīng was truly loyal to Wèi.
But the "Shì Yǔ" states he was upright,
and then claims it was due to Shěn
and Yè expressing his intentions,
how contradictory is that?
Therefore, the words of these two families are deeply appreciated.
Shān Gōng and Jī
and Ruǎn met once,

Shān's wife, Madam Hán,
felt that her husband's relationship with those two was different from ordinary friendships,

Shān said:
"The only two men I could be friends with back then

His wife said:

Another day,
the two men came,

That night, she pierced a hole in the wall to watch them,

Shān entered and said:
"What do you think of the two men?"
His wife said:
"Your talent and ability are far inferior to theirs,

The duke said,
"Those fellows also usually consider my judgment to be superior."
The *Jin Yangqiu* says:
"Tāo (陶) was naturally refined and open-minded,

Wáng Yǐn's *Jin Shu* says:

Wáng Hún's wife, Lady Zhōng, gave birth to a virtuous daughter.
Yú Yù's *Jin Shu* says:
Hún zì Xuánchōng,

There was a son of a military family,

The *Wáng Shì Pǔ* (Genealogy of the Wáng Family) says:

She said:

After a while,

Wǔzǐ said:

His mother said:

If he doesn't live a long life,
bù dé shēn qí cái yòng. (Unable to fully utilize his talents.)
guān qí xíng gǔ, (Observing his physical form and bone structure,)
bì bù shòu, (he surely will not live long,)
bù kě yǔ hūn." (he is not suitable for marriage.")
Wǔzǐ cóng zhī. (Wǔzǐ followed his advice.)
Bīng ér shù nián guǒ wáng. (The "soldier boy" indeed died a few years later.)
Jiǎ Chōng qián fù, (Jiǎ Chōng's previous wife,)
shì Lǐ Fēng nǚ. (was the daughter of Lǐ Fēng.)
Fēng bèi zhū, (When Lǐ Fēng was executed,)
líhūn xǐ biān. (she was divorced and exiled to the border regions.)
"Fùrén Jí" yuē: ("Collection of Women" says:)

Fēng zhū, (After Lǐ Fēng was executed,)
xǐ Lè Làng." (she was exiled to Lelang.)
Hòu yù shè dé huán, (Later, she was pardoned and allowed to return,)
Chōng xiān yǐ qǔ Guō Pèi nǚ. (but Chōng had already taken the daughter of Guō Pèi.)
"Jiǎ Shì Pǔ" yuē: ("Genealogy of the Jiǎ Clan" says:)

jí Guǎngxuān Jūn yě." (that is, the Lady of Guǎngxuān.")
Wǔdì tè tīng zhì zuǒyòu fūrén. (Emperor Wǔ specially permitted him to have both a left and right wife.)
Lǐ shì bié zhù wài, (The Lǐ woman lived separately outside [his residence],)

"Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" yuē: ("Eulogies of the Dukes of Jin" says:)

ér Qí Xiàn Wáng fēi yù lìng Chōng yí Guō shì, (and the Consort of the Prince Xiàn of Qí wanted Chōng to abandon the Guō woman,)
Furthermore, he wanted to take her mother as a concubine.
Chōng did not allow it.
He built a residence for the Lǐ family,
but did not visit them.
Chōng's mother, Liǔ Shì, was about to die.
Chōng asked if she had any last words.
Liǔ said:
"I told you to welcome the new bride of the Lǐ family, but you were unwilling.

Lady Guō said to Chōng:

Chōng said:

The *Chōng Bié Zhuàn* says:

Thereupon, Lady Guō arranged grand regalia,
and brought many serving maids.
Once she arrived,

the Lǐ family woman rose to greet her.
Guō involuntarily bent her legs,

After returning,

Chōng said:
"Didn't I tell you what she was like?"
According to the *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn*, it says:
"Shìzǔ (世祖) considered that Lǐ Fēng (李豐) had offended the Jìn (晉) court,

"Since Chōng (充) had broken off the marriage with the Lǐ (李) family,

Lǐ's (李) imprisonment was lifted,

Chōng's (充) mother, Liǔ (柳), also ordered Chōng (充) to welcome Lǐ (李).
Huái (槐) was furious,
raised her arms and reproached Chōng (充), saying:
'Establishing laws and ordinances
and contributing to the establishment of the dynasty
I have my share in that!
How can Lǐ (李) be on par with me?'
Thereupon, Chōng (充) built a house in Yǒngnián (永年) neighborhood to settle Lǐ (李).
Huái (槐) found out about it later.
Whenever Chōng (充) went out,
she would always send people to look for him.

*Jìn Zàn* (晉贊) states that Shìzǔ (世祖) issued an edict not to send Lǐ (李) back,

Chōng (充) feared the Guō (郭) family,
and dared not welcome Lǐ (李).
The three accounts are not the same;
it is not clear which is correct.
However, Lǐ shì did not return,

Yet the *Shìshuō* says
she "simply refused to return,"
which is wrong.
Moreover, Guō Huái was forceful and fierce;
how could she condescend to bow to Lǐ on his behalf?
All of this is false.
Jǐa Chōng's wife, Lǐ shì, wrote *Nǚ Xùn* (Instructions for Women),

Lǐ shì's daughter

After Empress Jǐa was deposed,

The daughter she bore, Hé,

After the marriage,

"Hǎo Zhòngjiàng of Xiāngchéng,

Lǐ Píngyáng,
Master of Qínzhōu,

"Kāng, courtesy name Xuánzhòu,
was from Jiāngxià,

A famous scholar of the Central Plains.
At the time, he was compared to Wáng Yífǔ.
Initially, Sūn Xiù wanted to establish his authority and power,

"Yuè Lìng is respected by the people and cannot be killed,

"Eulogies of the Dukes of Jìn" says:
"Sūn Xiù, courtesy name Jùnzhōng,

Initially, when Zhòng was at home,

When Zhōu Jùn was serving as General Who Pacifies the East (Āndōng),

Her father and brothers agreed to it.

Tóu Kǎn stayed overnight.

Kǎn's mother, Zhàn Shì, said to Kǎn:

Zhàn's hair was piled on the ground,

By evening,
she had prepared a fine meal,

Kuí was not only impressed by her talent and eloquence,
but also deeply ashamed of her generosity.
The next morning, he left,
and Kǎn kept seeing him off,

Kuí said:
"The road is already long,
you should return."
Kǎn still did not turn back,
Kuí said:
"You may go now!
When I get to Luòyáng,

Kǎn then returned.
Kuí arrived in Luò,

Gù Róng, and others.
gaining great commendation.

Emperor Míng of the Jìn 晉明帝 was versed in interpreting graves and residences.
Hearing that Guō Pú 郭璞 was conducting a burial for someone,

He then asked the owner:

Guō Jǐngchún crossed the river,

Jǐngchún said:

Now, the sand has risen,

Within a few days,
Guǒ zhèn bǎi fěnsuì,

Wáng Yǐn's *Book of Jin* says:

The Grand General said:

Huán Gōng had a chief clerk skilled at distinguishing wine,

Wén yú Fǎ Kāi yǒu míng,

After he arrived,

After taking one dose,

There was a servant regularly employed,

Hào was moved by his profound filial piety,

Yáng Chánghé, Yáng Chánghé, was erudite and skilled in calligraphy.

Contains the essay "Head's Rebuke to Zǐ Yǔ," which says:

The text says:
"In the first year of the Tàishǐ era,

I planted hair and skin for you,
To place the nose and ears,
to affix the eyebrows and beard,
to insert the teeth,
the pupils emanate light,

Every time I enter or exit,
roaming and playing in the marketplace,
those who walk give way,
those who sit straighten up in awe.
Some call me "Your Lordship" (Jūnhóu),
some say "General" (Jiāngjūn),
cupping their hands and leaning to the side,
standing in awkward places.
Such is the greatness of my form.
You wear no crown or cap,
you wear no gold or silver,
you use a hairpin as a fastener,
you use a cap to replace a headscarf,
you do not taste delicacies,
eating only grain and vegetables,
crouching and stooping in the garden,
covered in dirt and sweat,
as the years pass,
you never regret it.
You are disgusted by my appearance,
and I despise your demeanor.
If this is the case,
it must be a burden on your conduct.
It must be that you are burdening yourself with your conduct.
You treat me as an enemy,
and I regard you as a foe.
Living like this is constantly joyless,
and both of us are distressed.
How base is this!
If you desire to be a treasure to people,
then you should be like Gāo Yáo,
Hòu Jì,
Wū Xián,
Yī Zhí,
protecting and assisting the royal house,
and be forever granted fiefs and flourishing.
If you desire to have a lofty reputation,
then you should be like Xǔ Yóu,
Zǐ Zāng,
Biàn Suí,
Wù Guāng,
washing their ears and fleeing from emoluments,
their fragrance flowing for a thousand years.
If you desire to be a persuader,
then you should be like Chén Zhěn,
Kuǎi Tōng,
Lù Shēng,
Dèng Gōng,
turning misfortune into fortune,
making their words smooth and eloquent.
If you desire to be ambitious and striving,
Then one should be like Jiǎ Shēng seeking an opportunity to prove himself,
or Zhōng Jūn requesting to be sent on a mission.
Sharpening their talents and abilities,
to serve in matters of state.
If you desire to be serene and detached,
then you should be like Lǎo Dān, guarding the One,
or Zhuāng Zhōu, finding contentment in his own way.
Expanding your mind and distancing yourself from desires,
with your aspirations reaching for the clouds and the sun.
If you desire to live in seclusion,

lingering in the sacred hills,

This is how a solitary individual can make himself known and achieve fame.
Now, you neither aspire to high moral principles,
nor do you follow the teachings of Confucianism or Mohism.
You are stuck in poverty and lowliness,

Observing your feelings,
and seeing your aspirations,
you retreat without becoming a recluse,

Is this not going too far?"
Thereupon, Zǐ Yǔ solemnly pondered and replied:

See what one sees,
and not see what one does not see.
Look at what one looks at,
and leave behind what one does not look at.
If they are like that which they resemble,
there is something more valuable than a horse."
Soon after,
the horse indeed proved to be a steed of a thousand *lǐ*.
Xiè Gōng said,
"There were no such two phrases at all;
Péi himself made up these words!"
Yǔ greatly disapproved of this,
and consequently presented Chén Dōngtíng's "Rhapsody on Passing Under the Wine Shop."
After reading it,
he did not offer any commendation or judgement,
but directly said,
"You are again composing like Péi!"
Because of this, *Yǔlín* was abandoned.
What exists now
was all written earlier,
and does not contain Xiè's words.
*Xù Jìn Yángqiū* says:
"During the Lónghé period of the Jìn Dynasty,
Péi Qǐ of Hédōng compiled from the Hàn and
Wèi dynasties up to the present time,
commendable words and responses,
calling it *Yǔlín*.
People at the time mostly liked this subject,
and the text consequently became popular.
Later, the account of the Grand Tutor's affairs was inaccurate,
and someone at Xiè's gathering recounted the Yellow Duke's wine shop.
Sītú Wáng Xuán composed a rhapsody for it,
and Xiè Gōng added that he was displeased with Wáng,
then said,
"You are again acting like Péi Láng learning."
From then on, everyone despised the matter.
A person from Ānxiāng who had resigned from his position as magistrate of Zhōngsù County went to see Ān.
Ān asked about his returning assets.
He replied,
"Lǐngnán is desolate and impoverished,
and I only have fifty thousand pūkuí palm-leaf fans,
which are also sluggish goods because it is the wrong season."
Ān then took one of the better ones and held it in his hand.
Thereupon, the scholars and commoners of the capital competed to admire and wear them.
The price increased several times,
and within ten days, they were all sold out.
What one loves grows feathers;
what one hates becomes sores and wounds.
A single word from Chancellor Xiè
can ruin a good reputation for a thousand years,
and whatever he favors
can elevate a false price to a hundred gold pieces.
How can one not be careful about the loves, hates, giving, and taking of those above! "
Wáng Běi, the Central Director, was not known by Lín Gōng.
Thereupon, he composed "A Discourse on Why Monks Cannot be Considered Lofty Scholars."
The gist of it said:
"Lofty scholars must be characterized by unrestrained hearts and harmonious resonance.
Monks, although claiming to be outside the secular world,
are instead bound by doctrines,
which is not what is meant by the free attainment of one's nature."
Someone asked Gù Chángkāng,
"Why don't you compose 'Odes to the Scholars of Luoyang'?"
He replied:
"Why stoop to creating the sound of an old maidservant!"
The Odes of the Scholars of Luòxià,
had a heavy and turbid tone,
hence the saying "sound of an old maidservant."
Yīn Yǐ and
Yǔ Héng were both maternal grandsons of Xiè Zhènxī.
The *Xiè Clan Genealogy* states:
"The eldest daughter, Sēngyào, married Yǔ Hé,
and the second daughter, Sēngsháo, married Yīn Xīn."
Yīn was insightful from a young age,
but Yǔ often did not acknowledge this.
Once, they together visited Lord Xiè,
who stared intently at Yīn and said:
"Ā Cháo really resembles Zhènxī."
Cháo was Yīn Yǐ's childhood name.
Thereupon, Yǔ lowered his voice and said:
"What is Dìng (定) like?"
Xiè Gōng (謝公) continued and replied,
"His cheeks are like Zhèn Xī's (鎮西)."
Yǔ (庾) then said,
"The cheeks are similar,
but are his feet vigorous?"
*Yǔ Shì Pǔ* (庾氏譜) says:
"Héng (恒)'s courtesy name was Jìngzé (敬則),
his grandfather was Liàng (亮),
and his father was Hé (龢).
Héng (恒) served and rose to the position of Vice President of the Ministry of Personnel."
People used to comment on Hán Kāngbó (韓康伯):
"His elbows lack elegance and spirit."
*Shuō Lín* (說林) says:
"Fàn Qǐ (范啟) said,
'Hán Kāngbó (韓康伯) is like a fleshy duck.'"
Fú Hóng (符宏) rebelled and came to surrender.
Grand Tutor Xiè (謝太傅) always welcomed and guided him.
Hóng (宏), considering himself talented,
often looked down on others,
and no one in the gathering refuted him.
It happened that Wáng Zǐyóu (王子猷) came,
and the Grand Tutor had them talk together.
Zǐyóu (子猷) stared at him directly for a long time,
then turned and said to the Grand Tutor:
"He is ultimately no different from other people!"
Hóngdà retired, ashamed.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Hóng
was Fú Jiān's son and heir.
He was killed by Yáo Cháng.
Hóng brought his mother and wife to surrender,
and an imperial edict granted him land and a residence.
Huán Xuán appointed Hóng as a general.
When Xuán was defeated,
he raided Xiāngzhōng
and was executed."
Zhī Dàolín, upon arriving in the east,
met the Wáng Zǐyóu brothers.
Upon returning, someone asked,
"What were the Wáng like?"
He replied,
"I saw a flock of white-necked crows,
only hearing them croak 'ah, ah.'"
Wáng Zhōngláng nominated Xǔ Xuándù for the position of Vice Minister of Personnel.
Xī Chóngxī said,
"The Chancellor (Xiàng Wáng) is a lover of good,
but Ā Nè (阿訥) should not be allowed to sit in court."
Nè was Xún's childhood name.
Wáng Xīngdào said,
"Xiè Wàngcài is flustered, like a falconer who has lost his hawk."
The *Yongjia Ji* says:
"Wáng Hézhī, courtesy name Xīngdào,
was a native of Lángyá.
His grandfather was Yì,
General Who Pacifies the South.
His father was Húzhī,
Governor of Sizhou.
Hézhī successively held the posts of Grand Administrator of Yongjia and
Regular Attendant."
Wàng Cài
was the childhood name of Xiè Yǎn.
Huán, the Prefect of Nán Commandery, whenever he saw someone displeased him,
would often angrily say:
"If you got a pear from the mourning family,
would you not steam it and eat it?"
An old saying:
"In Mòlíng, there were the pears of the mourning Zhòng family, which were very beautiful,
as large as a *sheng* measure,
and dissolved upon entering the mouth.
It means that a foolish person does not distinguish flavors
and steams and eats a good pear."
Deception, Chapter Twenty-Seven
When Wèi Wǔ was young,
he once liked to act as a wandering swordsman with Yuán Shào.
Observing someone's wedding,
they then secretly entered the host's garden.
During the night, someone shouted:
"There are thieves!"
People in the green tent all came out to watch.
Wèi Wǔ then entered,
drew his blade, and kidnapped the new bride. With Shào, he went back out.
Losing their way,
they fell into a thicket of citrus thorns.
Shào couldn't move.
He shouted loudly again, saying:
"The thieves are here!"
Shào, in a state of panic, threw himself out [of the thicket],
and thus they both escaped.
The *Cáo Mán Zhuàn* says:
"Cāo's childhood name was Ā Mán.
In his youth, he liked trickery
and was unrestrained and undisciplined."
Sūn Shèng's *Zá Yǔ* says:
"Wǔ Wáng was fond of chivalry in his youth
and was dissolute, not cultivating any profession.
He once secretly entered the residence of Regular Attendant Zhāng Ràng.
Ràng took up a hand-halberd in the courtyard
and climbed over the wall and out.
He had extraordinary strength,
so no one could harm him."
Wèi Wǔ was on campaign,
and they lost the source of water.
The whole army was thirsty.
Then he gave an order, saying:
"Ahead there is a large plum grove,
with abundant fruit,
sweet and sour,
which can quench our thirst."
When the soldiers heard this,
their mouths all watered,
and taking advantage of this, they were able to reach the front spring.
Wèi Wǔ (魏武, referring to Cáo Cāo 曹操) often said:
"When someone wants to harm me,
I always feel a stirring in my heart."
Thereupon, he said to a trusted petty man:
"You conceal a knife and secretly come to my side,
I will surely say that I feel a stirring in my heart.
I will seize you and have you executed,
but you must not reveal who sent you,
no harm will come to you,
and I will reward you generously!"
The man who was to be seized believed him,
and was not afraid.
Consequently, he was executed.
This man did not know [the truth] even in death.
Those around Cáo Cāo thought it was real,
and those plotting rebellion had their spirits dampened.
The *Cáo Mán Zhuàn* (曹瞞傳) says:
"When Cāo (操, referring to Cáo Cāo 曹操) was in the army,
the grain supply was insufficient,
he privately spoke to the person in charge, saying:
'What should we do?'
The person in charge said:
'We can use smaller measures to make it sufficient.'
Cāo (操, referring to Cáo Cāo 曹操) said:
'Good.'"
Later, the army murmured that Cáo Cāo was deceiving them.
Cáo Cāo labeled the officer in charge,
paraded him around with his back exposed, and announced:
"He used small measures
to steal grain from the army."
Then he executed him.
He further said:
"I am only borrowing your death
to appease the hearts of the multitude."
All his deceptions were of this kind."
Wèi Wǔ (魏武), referring to Cáo Cāo, often said:
"You must not recklessly approach me while I am sleeping.
If you approach, I will strike people,
and I will not even realize it.
Those around me should be very careful of this!"
Later, he feigned sleep.
One of his favored attendants secretly covered him with a blanket.
Thereupon, he immediately struck and killed him.
From then on, whenever he slept,
no one dared to approach him.
When Yuán Shào (袁紹) was young,
he once sent someone to throw a sword at Wèi Wǔ (魏武) at night.
It landed a little lower
and did not hit.
Wèi Wǔ (魏武) measured it,
thinking that the next time it would certainly be higher.
